### Problem: Diagonal traverse {#sec-mat-p1-diag}

::: {.p-statement}
Return all cells of an $m \times n$ matrix in diagonal order, zig-zagging: the diagonals are the sets of cells sharing $i+j$, visited for $s = 0, 1, \dots, m+n-2$. Even-indexed diagonals are read bottom-left to top-right (going "up"), odd-indexed ones top-right to bottom-left (going "down").

$1 \le m, n \le 10^4$ and $1 \le m \cdot n \le 10^4$; cells are integers. On `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]` the answer is `[1,2,4,7,5,3,6,8,9]`. On `[[1,2],[3,4]]` the answer is `[1,2,3,4]`.

Source: [LC 498 · Diagonal Traverse](https://leetcode.com/problems/diagonal-traverse/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Every anti-diagonal is pinned by one number, $s = i + j$ (@sec-mat-a2), so the matrix is a stack of $m + n - 1$ bands $s = 0, 1, \dots, m+n-2$. The zig-zag is a property of the band, not of any cell: read band $s$ upward (bottom-left to top-right) when $s$ is even and downward when $s$ is odd.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Bucket by $i+j$.** Put every cell into `buckets[i + j]` in row-major order (so each bucket lists its band top to bottom, the downward direction), then emit the buckets in order, reversing the even ones. $O(mn)$ extra memory.
2. **Pointer walk.** Drop the buckets: a head $(i,j)$ rides the current band and, when the next step would leave the grid, hops to the start of the next band and flips a direction bit. $O(1)$ extra memory.
3. **Band sweep.** Compute each band's cells from its bounds: rows $i = \max(0, s-(n-1)) \dots \min(s, m-1)$ with $j = s - i$, reversed when $s$ is even. No direction bit and no hop rules.

**Invariant.** After band $s$ is emitted, the output holds exactly the cells with $i + j \le s$, each once, so after band $m+n-2$ it holds all $mn$ cells.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Bucket by $i+j$

::: {.form-next}
Sort every cell into `buckets[i + j]`, then for each band emit it forwards on odd $s$ and reversed on even $s$. $O(mn)$ time and space, and the reverse-when-even rule is stated in one line. This is the rung that makes the parity invariant visible.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("diagtraverse", "bucket")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
from collections import defaultdict


def diag_bucket(M):
    R, C = len(M), len(M[0])
    buckets = defaultdict(list)
    for i in range(R):
        for j in range(C):
            buckets[i + j].append(M[i][j])
    out = []
    for s in range(R + C - 1):
        band = buckets[s]
        out += band[::-1] if s % 2 == 0 else band
    return out


assert diag_bucket([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]
assert diag_bucket([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert diag_bucket([[1, 2, 3]]) == [1, 2, 3]
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> diagBucket(vector<vector<int>>& M) {
    int R = M.size(), C = M[0].size();
    vector<vector<int>> bucket(R + C - 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < R; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < C; ++j)
            bucket[i + j].push_back(M[i][j]);
    vector<int> out;
    for (int s = 0; s < R + C - 1; ++s) {
        if (s % 2 == 0)
            for (int k = (int)bucket[s].size() - 1; k >= 0; --k) out.push_back(bucket[s][k]);
        else
            for (int v : bucket[s]) out.push_back(v);
    }
    return out;
}
```

:::

#### Pointer walk

::: {.form-next}
Drop the buckets. A head $(i,j)$ rides the current diagonal until it would leave the grid, then hops onto the next band and flips direction. Up-right: at the last column step down, at the top step right, otherwise $i{-}1, j{+}1$. Down-left: at the last row step right, at the first column step down, otherwise $i{+}1, j{-}1$. $O(1)$ extra space, and the hop rules are exactly the picture in @sec-mat-a2.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("diagtraverse", "walk")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def diag_walk(M):
    R, C = len(M), len(M[0])
    r = c = 0
    up = True
    out = []
    for _ in range(R * C):
        out.append(M[r][c])
        if up:
            if c == C - 1:
                up = False; r += 1
            elif r == 0:
                up = False; c += 1
            else:
                r -= 1; c += 1
        else:
            if r == R - 1:
                up = True; c += 1
            elif c == 0:
                up = True; r += 1
            else:
                r += 1; c -= 1
    return out


assert diag_walk([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]
assert diag_walk([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
for _ in range(80):
    R, C = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    M = [[a * C + b for b in range(C)] for a in range(R)]
    assert diag_walk(M) == diag_bucket(M)
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> diagWalk(vector<vector<int>>& M) {
    int R = M.size(), C = M[0].size(), r = 0, c = 0;
    bool up = true;
    vector<int> out;
    for (int k = 0; k < R * C; ++k) {
        out.push_back(M[r][c]);
        if (up) {
            if (c == C - 1) { up = false; ++r; }
            else if (r == 0) { up = false; ++c; }
            else { --r; ++c; }
        } else {
            if (r == R - 1) { up = true; ++c; }
            else if (c == 0) { up = true; ++r; }
            else { ++r; --c; }
        }
    }
    return out;
}
```

:::

#### Band sweep

::: {.form-next}
For each band $s$, its cells run over the row range $i = \max(0, s-(C-1)) \dots \min(s, R-1)$ with $j = s - i$. Read them in that row order (which is down-left) and reverse when $s$ is even. No `seen`, no buckets, no direction bit — one loop per band straight from the bounds — which is why people reach for it in a contest.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("diagtraverse", "sweep")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def diag_sweep(M):
    R, C = len(M), len(M[0])
    out = []
    for s in range(R + C - 1):
        i0, i1 = max(0, s - (C - 1)), min(s, R - 1)
        band = [M[i][s - i] for i in range(i0, i1 + 1)]
        out += band[::-1] if s % 2 == 0 else band
    return out


assert diag_sweep([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9]
assert diag_sweep([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert diag_sweep([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) == [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6]
for _ in range(80):
    R, C = random.randint(1, 5), random.randint(1, 5)
    M = [[a * C + b for b in range(C)] for a in range(R)]
    assert diag_sweep(M) == diag_walk(M) == diag_bucket(M)
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> diagSweep(vector<vector<int>>& M) {
    int R = M.size(), C = M[0].size();
    vector<int> out;
    for (int s = 0; s < R + C - 1; ++s) {
        int i0 = max(0, s - (C - 1)), i1 = min(s, R - 1);
        vector<int> band;
        for (int i = i0; i <= i1; ++i) band.push_back(M[i][s - i]);
        if (s % 2 == 0) reverse(band.begin(), band.end());
        for (int v : band) out.push_back(v);
    }
    return out;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
All three are $\Theta(mn)$ time. **Bucket** and **band sweep** allocate $O(mn)$ (the buckets) or $O(\min(m,n))$ per band (the sweep's temporary list); the **pointer walk** is $O(1)$ auxiliary. With $m \cdot n \le 10^4$ all fit easily; the pointer walk is the one to memorise because it needs no extra container at all.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A single row or column has every cell on its own band ($s = j$ or $s = i$), so all three rungs emit the row straight, and the reverse-when-even still keeps a $1 \times n$ in left-to-right order because each band holds one cell.
- The band count is $m + n - 1$, not $\min(m,n)$; the corner bands $s = 0$ and $s = m+n-2$ hold exactly one cell.
- A $2 \times 3$ matrix sweeps `1 2 4 5 3 6` — good for checking the even/odd direction flip on a non-square.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Reversing the wrong parity.** Even $s$ is the up-right band; reversing the odd bands instead gives `1 4 2 3 5 7 ...`, wrong from the first band of length two.
- **Band row range off by one.** `i1 = min(s, R-1)` and `i0 = max(0, s-(C-1))`; using `i0 = s - C` (no minus one) reads a column index of $C$, out of bounds.
- **Walking past the last cell.** The pointer walk must stop after exactly $mn$ emissions; a `while r < R and c < C` loop drops the tail cells reached by a hop.
:::

**Variants.** Spiral Matrix (@sec-mat-p1-spiral) is the sibling traversal, where the moving boundary is a ring rather than a band. [LC 1424 · Diagonal Traverse II](https://leetcode.com/problems/diagonal-traverse-ii/){difficulty="Medium"} has ragged rows (no rectangle), which kills the band sweep and the pointer walk but not the buckets: key each cell by $i + j$ and read each bucket bottom-up. Grouping by the *other* key $i - j$ (the top-left to bottom-right diagonals) is the tool of @sec-mat-p5.

**Try it.** Group the cells by $i - j$ and print each diagonal top-left to bottom-right; on the $3 \times 3$ sample that is `[3] [2,6] [1,5,9] [4,8] [7]`.
